title: UI Design with Figma
subtitle: Design polished, buildable app screens in Figma with a reusable component system, a tappable prototype and a clean developer handoff.
description: An advanced, hands-on course in the craft of interface design. You build one practice app from file setup to handoff: resizable layouts with auto layout, foundations for spacing, type and colour, a component library with variants and properties, an interactive prototype, accessibility checks and specs. You finish by learning to scope, price and present UI work to clients and employers.
outcomes: Build mobile screens with frames, constraints and nested auto layout that resize correctly from 360 px upwards
Define spacing, type scale and colour role foundations and save them as styles or variables
Create a component library with variants and boolean, text and instance swap properties
Wire an interactive prototype with overlays, fixed bars and Smart Animate, and test it on a phone
Run contrast and target-size checks against WCAG 2.2 AA and prepare a developer handoff
Turn discovery into a screen inventory, an itemised price and a portfolio case study
audience: Women who already understand basic UX (flows and wireframes) and want to produce professional, developer-ready interface designs for clients or employers.
tools: A laptop or desktop computer (Figma design work is very hard on a phone alone)
A free Figma account (Starter plan) in the browser or desktop app
The Figma mobile app on your Android or iPhone to test prototypes
Stable internet access; designs are stored online
A notebook or spreadsheet for estimates and case study notes

modules.title: Figma Foundations: Files, Layout and Visual Craft
modules.overview: You move from a UX flow to real, buildable screens. You set up a professional Figma file, build layouts that resize correctly with frames, constraints and auto layout, and define the spacing, type and colour foundations every later screen will use.

lessons.title: From UX flow to polished UI: the Figma workspace and a professional file
objectives: Explain what a UI designer hands over that a UX flow or wireframe does not
Find your way around the Figma canvas, layers panel, toolbar and properties panel
Set up a Figma file with pages and sections a client or developer can follow
Use the ten keyboard shortcuts that save the most time in daily UI work

blocks.text: A UX flow tells you **what** a product must do: which screens exist and how a person moves between them. A wireframe shows the rough layout in grey boxes. **UI design** turns that into the exact interface a developer will build: real colours, real fonts, exact spacing in pixels, every button state, and a clickable prototype. This course assumes you already understand basic UX ideas (users, flows, wireframes). Here we focus on the craft of building the interface itself in Figma, to a standard that holds up when a developer opens the file.

Figma is a design tool that runs in a web browser, with desktop apps for Windows and macOS and a mobile app for viewing designs and prototypes on a phone. Because files live online, a client in Lagos, a developer in Nairobi and you in Abuja can open the same file at the same time and see each other's cursors. That is the main reason teams use it: one shared source of truth instead of screenshots sent back and forth on WhatsApp.

blocks.name: design-tools
blocks.alt: A designer arranging interface elements with design tools
blocks.caption: In this course Figma is your workbench: every screen, component and prototype lives in one shared file.

blocks.text: What a finished UI handover contains

items: **Screens** for every step of the flow, at the real device size, including empty, loading and error states.
**Foundations**: the colour, type, spacing and corner-radius values the screens use, saved as styles or variables.
**Components**: buttons, inputs, cards and navigation built once and reused, with all their states.
**A prototype** that links the screens so a client can tap through the experience.
**Specs and assets**: named layers, exportable icons and images, and notes a developer can read without calling you.

blocks.text: The Figma workspace in four parts

head: Area
Where
What you do there
rows: Bottom of the screen in the current Figma layout (top in older versions)
Pick tools: Move (V), Frame (F), Rectangle (R), Text (T), Pen (P), Comment (C)
See pages and every layer in order; rename, lock, hide and nest layers
The endless board where frames (screens) sit side by side
Exact size, position, auto layout, fill, stroke, effects and export settings for whatever is selected; tabs switch to Prototype

blocks.text: A **frame** is Figma's container for a screen or any section of one. Unlike a simple group, a frame has its own size, background, clipping and layout rules, and it can become a component. When you press **F**, the right panel offers device presets such as Android Compact (412 × 917) and iPhone 16 (393 × 852). Pick a preset that matches the main device of your users, and remember that many low-cost Android phones in Nigeria have screens about 360 points wide, so always check your layout at that width too.
Shortcuts worth learning in week one

head: Shortcut (Windows / Mac)
Action
rows: Add auto layout to the selection
Ctrl + Alt + K / Cmd + Option + K
Ctrl + Alt + G / Cmd + Option + G
Wrap the selection in a frame
Switch Dev Mode on or off (paid plans)
Measure the distance between two layers
Zoom to fit everything on the page

blocks.title: From flow to handover
items: UX flow and wireframes
Visual foundations
Components
Final screens
Prototype
Developer handover
blocks.caption: Each stage in this course feeds the next, so foundations and components come before final screens.

blocks.text: Organise the file before you design

Clients and developers judge your professionalism the moment they open the file. A tidy structure also saves you hours when changes arrive. Use **pages** for the big parts of the project and **sections** (Shift + S) on a page to group related screens. Name everything in plain words. A layer called "Rectangle 47" tells nobody anything; a layer called "Price tag" does.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting up the practice file for a market ordering app
blocks.context: Throughout this course you will design a practice concept called Oja Fresh, an app for ordering foodstuff (tomatoes, pepper, rice, garri) from a local market for home delivery. This is an invented practice brief, not a real company. Here is how Amaka, for example, sets up the file on day one.
steps: Creates a new design file and names it "Oja Fresh, UI v1".
Adds six pages: Cover, Foundations, Components, Screens, Prototype, Archive.
On the Cover page draws a 1600 × 960 frame with the project name, her name, the date and a status label "In progress", so the file thumbnail is readable in the file browser.
On the Screens page creates four sections: Onboarding, Browse and search, Cart and checkout, Orders and profile.
Places one Android Compact frame (412 × 917) in the Browse section, names it "Home / Default" and adds a second 360 × 800 frame named "Home / Small phone" to test narrow screens.
Moves old experiments to Archive instead of deleting them, so nothing useful is lost.
blocks.result: In about 15 minutes she has a file anyone can navigate: a developer opening it later can find every checkout screen in one section without asking her.

blocks.title: Name screens by flow and state
blocks.text: Use the pattern Flow / Screen / State, for example "Checkout / Delivery address / Error". Screens then sort together in the layers panel and the developer instantly sees which state each one shows.

Finally, learn where Figma keeps your safety net. **Version history** (File menu, Show version history) lets you name a checkpoint, such as "Sent to client 1", and return to it later. Comments (C) keep feedback attached to the exact element it is about, which is far easier to track than a long voice note. Get into the habit of saving a named version before every client review.

takeaways: UI design turns flows into exact, buildable screens with states, components, a prototype and specs.
Frames are real containers with size, clipping and layout rules; groups are not.
Organise with pages, sections and plain names such as Flow / Screen / State.
Save a named version before every review so you can always go back.

activity.title: Set up your practice file
steps: Create a free Figma account and a new design file for your own practice app idea (or use Oja Fresh).
Add the six pages: Cover, Foundations, Components, Screens, Prototype, Archive.
Build a cover frame with the project name, your name, date and status.
Create at least three sections on the Screens page, one per main flow, with one named frame in each.
Save a named version called "File set up".
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your layers panel showing the pages, sections and named frames, plus the cover frame.

lessons.title: Frames, constraints and auto layout: screens that resize correctly
objectives: Choose between groups, frames and auto layout frames for a given job
Set constraints so elements stay in place when a screen gets wider
Build nested auto layout with correct gap, padding and resizing (hug, fill, fixed)
Add a 4-column layout grid for mobile screens

blocks.text: A beginner's screen looks fine at one size and breaks at every other. A professional screen keeps working when the phone is wider, when a product name is longer than expected, or when the client adds one more item. Three Figma features make that possible: **constraints**, **auto layout** and **layout grids**. This lesson teaches all three on real parts of the Oja Fresh app.

blocks.name: responsive
blocks.alt: The same interface shown on a phone, tablet and laptop
blocks.caption: Constraints and auto layout let one design adapt to different screen widths instead of breaking.

blocks.text: Groups, frames and auto layout frames

head: Container
Use it for
Watch out
rows: Quickly moving a few loose items together
Has no size or rules of its own; it just wraps its children
Screens, cards, anything with a background, clipping or constraints
Children use constraints to decide how they move when the frame resizes
Lists, buttons, cards, nav bars: anything that stacks in a row or column
Children follow the gap and padding rules, not constraints

blocks.text: Constraints: pinning elements to edges

Select a layer inside a frame and the Constraints section shows horizontal options (Left, Right, Left and right, Center, Scale) and vertical options (Top, Bottom, Top and bottom, Center, Scale). A cart icon in the top right corner should be **Right** and **Top**, so it stays in the corner when the screen widens. A search bar should be **Left and right**, so it stretches. A bottom navigation bar should be **Left and right** plus **Bottom**. Test by dragging the edge of the frame: whatever moves wrongly needs a different constraint.
Auto layout: the core professional skill

Auto layout turns a frame into a flexible stack, similar to how a web developer lays out a page with CSS flexbox. You choose a **direction** (vertical, horizontal or wrap), a **gap** between items, **padding** around the inside edges and **alignment**. Each child, and the frame itself, then gets a resizing rule:

items: **Hug contents**: the frame shrinks or grows to fit what is inside. A button that hugs its label grows when "Add" becomes "Add to cart".
**Fill container**: the child stretches to take the space its parent gives it. A product card's text column fills the width beside the image.
**Fixed**: an exact size that does not change, such as a 64 × 64 product photo.
Text layers also have **Auto width**, **Auto height**, **Fixed size** and **Truncate text**; long product names in a card usually need Auto height or Truncate with a maximum number of lines.

blocks.title: Fixed layout versus auto layout
items: Manual frame
Auto layout frame
left: You move each item by hand
right: Items stack by gap and padding
blocks.caption: Auto layout replaces hand positioning with rules, which is why edits stay fast and consistent.

blocks.title: Worked example: an auto layout product card
blocks.context: For example, Amaka builds the product card for the Oja Fresh home screen on a 360-wide test frame with 16 px margins on each side, so the card must be 360 minus 16 minus 16 = 328 px wide.
steps: Draws a 64 × 64 rectangle for the photo, sets corner radius 8 and names it "Photo".

Types three text layers: "Fresh tomatoes (paint bucket)", "Mile 12 Market" and a sample price "₦6,500" (placeholder, not a real market price). Selects them and presses Shift + A to make a vertical stack with gap 4. Names it "Info".
Selects Photo and Info, presses Shift + A again for a horizontal stack with gap 12 and padding 12 on all sides. Names it "Product card" and gives it a white fill, radius 12 and a light grey stroke.

Sets the card's width to Fill container inside the screen's main vertical stack, and sets Info to Fill container so the text uses all remaining width: 328 minus 12 minus 12 padding minus 64 photo minus 12 gap = 228 px for text.
Sets the product name to Auto height with Truncate text after 2 lines, then pastes a very long name to test it.
Duplicates the card three times inside a vertical auto layout list with gap 12, then changes the test frame width from 360 to 412 to confirm every card stretches.
blocks.result: One card that adapts to any phone width and any product name. Changing the gap from 12 to 16 in one place re-spaces the whole list instantly.

blocks.text: Layout grids

A **layout grid** draws guide columns on a frame so content lines up across screens. A common mobile setup is **4 columns, 16 px margin, 16 px gutter**, which matches the compact layout guidance in Google's Material Design. Add it in the Layout guide (layout grid) section of a selected frame, set the type to Stretch, and save it as a style so every screen uses the same grid.

blocks.title: Absolute position for badges
blocks.text: Sometimes one child must ignore the stack, such as a red count badge on the cart icon. Select it and choose "Ignore auto layout" (absolute position), then use constraints to pin it to the top right of its parent.

blocks.title: Watch the video with a purpose
blocks.text: In the video below, pause after each auto layout step and repeat it in your own file. Watching without building does not build speed.

takeaways: Use frames for screens and cards, auto layout for anything that stacks, groups only for quick moves.
Constraints pin children to edges in normal frames; test them by resizing.
Hug, Fill and Fixed decide how each element responds to content and width.
Always test at 360 px as well as your main device width.

activity.title: Build a resizable list
steps: Build one product or service card for your practice app with nested auto layout (image plus text stack).
Make a vertical list of four cards with a fixed gap.
Add a top app bar whose search field uses Fill container and whose icons stay right aligned.
Resize the screen from 360 to 412 px wide and fix anything that breaks.
Paste a product name three times longer than normal and fix the text setting until the card still looks right.
activity.evidence: Two screenshots of the same screen at 360 px and 412 px wide, with the layers panel showing your auto layout frames.

lessons.title: Visual foundations: 8-point spacing, a type scale and colour roles for African mobile users
objectives: Apply an 8-point spacing system with a small set of approved values
Calculate a type scale and round it to practical sizes
Define colour roles (primary, surface, text, error) instead of loose swatches
Adapt foundations to real conditions: small screens, sunlight, data cost and local text

blocks.text: Polished interfaces feel calm because they repeat a small number of decisions. Professionals do not choose spacing, font sizes and colours screen by screen. They define **foundations** once and use them everywhere. In this lesson you set those foundations for Oja Fresh on the Foundations page of your file.

blocks.name: color-palette
blocks.alt: A person choosing colours from a palette
blocks.caption: Foundations such as colour roles, spacing and type are decided once and then reused across every screen.

blocks.text: Spacing on an 8-point system

Most product teams use an **8-point system**: spacing and sizes are multiples of 8, with 4 allowed for small gaps. A typical approved set is **4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48**. Inside a card you might use 12 padding and 4 or 8 between lines of text; between sections of a screen, 24 or 32. Because only these values are allowed, screens line up and developers can turn them into a short list of spacing tokens. Multiples of 4 and 8 also convert to whole pixels at 1.5x, 2x and 3x screen densities, which keeps edges crisp.
A type scale you can explain

A **type scale** is a short ladder of text sizes made by multiplying a base size by a fixed ratio. Body text on mobile is usually 16 to 17: Material Design's main body style is 16, and Apple's default body text is 17 points. We will use 16. With a ratio of 1.25 (called a major third) each step is 25 percent larger than the one below it.

blocks.title: Worked example: building the Oja Fresh type scale
blocks.context: For example, Amaka uses Inter, a free font built into Figma, with base size 16 and ratio 1.25.
steps: Step down once: 16 ÷ 1.25 = 12.8.
Rounds to even, easy numbers: 12.8 to 12 or 13 (she picks 13 for readability), 25 to 24, 31.25 to 32, 39.06 to 40.
Names the roles: Caption 13, Body 16, Title 20, Heading 24, Display 32. She keeps 40 in reserve and does not use it on mobile.
Sets line height to about 1.4 to 1.5 times the size for body text: 16 × 1.5 = 24 px. For headings she uses tighter line height: 24 × 1.25 = 30 px, rounded to 32 to stay on the 8-point grid.
Saves each as a Text style named Body/Regular, Body/Bold, Title, Heading, Display, Caption.
blocks.result: Six text styles cover every screen. If the client later wants bigger text, she edits Body once and every screen updates.

blocks.title: Type hierarchy on a mobile screen
items: Display 32: rare
Heading 24
Title 20
Body 16: most text
Caption 13
blocks.caption: Few large sizes at the top, most of the screen in body text, and small captions only for supporting details.

blocks.text: Colour roles, not just colours

Beginners save swatches named "Green 1" and "Nice orange". Professionals name colours by **role**, the job the colour does, so that a later rebrand changes values, not meaning. Material Design 3 uses this idea, with pairs such as primary and on-primary (text placed on primary). A useful starter set:

head: Role
Used for
Oja Fresh example value
rows: Main buttons, active tab, key links
Text and icons placed on primary
Supporting details such as market name

blocks.text: In Figma you can save these as **colour styles** or, better for growing systems, as **colour variables** in a collection named, for example, "Color". Variables can later hold a light and a dark value for the same role. You will check every text and background pair for contrast in Module 2; for now, choose a primary dark enough that white text on it is easy to read.
Designing for real conditions

items: **Small screens**: test every screen at 360 px wide. Keep tap targets at least 48 × 48 (Android guidance) or 44 × 44 points (Apple guidance).
**Bright sunlight**: users often check orders outdoors. Strong contrast and 16 px body text help far more than thin, pale grey text.
**Data cost**: every large photo costs the user money to load. Design layouts that still make sense with small thumbnails or a plain placeholder colour while images load.

**Local text**: test real words, not filler text. Yoruba and Igbo use tone marks (for example "ẹ̀fọ́"), Hausa uses hooked letters (ɓ, ɗ, ƙ), and English labels may be translated later and grow longer. Make sure your font supports the characters you need and that buttons hug their labels.
**Money formatting**: show naira as "₦6,500" with the naira sign and a thousands comma, and agree the format with the developer.

blocks.title: Check font character support
blocks.text: Not every free font contains Yoruba, Igbo or Hausa characters. Type the real words in Figma before you commit to a font. If you see empty boxes or letters falling back to another font, choose a different typeface.

takeaways: Use a small approved spacing set built on multiples of 8 (plus 4).
A type scale is base size × ratio, rounded to practical values and saved as text styles.
Name colours by role so a rebrand changes values, not meaning.
Design for 360 px screens, sunlight, data cost and real local text.

activity.title: Build your Foundations page
steps: Write your approved spacing values on the Foundations page as labelled boxes (4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32).
Calculate a type scale from 16 with ratio 1.2 or 1.25, show your arithmetic, round the values and save at least five text styles.
Create colour styles or variables for at least six roles with plain role names.
Type three real local words or product names (with tone marks if your users need them) in your chosen font and check they display correctly.
Apply your styles to the screen you built in the last lesson.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your Foundations page showing spacing, the type scale with arithmetic, and the named colour roles.

quiz.q: A client sends a wireframe and says, "So the UI is basically done?" Which item is part of a UI handover but usually missing from a wireframe?
options: The list of screens in the flow
Exact colours, type sizes, spacing and every button state
The order in which users move between screens
A rough idea of where the search bar sits
quiz.explain: Wireframes show structure. UI design adds exact visual values and states that a developer can build from.

quiz.q: Amaka's cart icon sits in the top right of a normal (non auto layout) frame. When the screen gets wider, the icon stays where it was and ends up in the middle. What should she change?
options: Set the icon's horizontal constraint to Right
Set the icon to Fill container
Group the icon with the title
quiz.explain: In a normal frame, constraints control how children move on resize. Right keeps the icon pinned to the right edge.

quiz.q: A product card is 328 px wide with 12 px padding on each side, a 64 px photo and a 12 px gap. How wide is the space left for the text column?
quiz.explain: 328 minus 12 minus 12 minus 64 minus 12 equals 228 px.

quiz.q: Using base 16 and ratio 1.25, what is the next size up after 20, before rounding?
quiz.explain: 20 × 1.25 = 25. You might then round it to 24 to fit the 8-point system.

quiz.q: Which colour style name will survive a rebrand best?
quiz.explain: Naming by role (Primary) means the value can change while every screen still uses the right colour for the job.

quiz.q: A button label changes from "Add" to "Add to cart" and now overflows. Which auto layout setting on the button frame fixes this?
quiz.explain: Hug contents lets the button grow or shrink to fit its label.

modules.title: Design Systems, Prototypes and Developer Handoff
modules.overview: You turn your foundations into a reusable component library, connect your screens into a prototype a client can tap through on a phone, and run the quality checks and handoff steps that let a developer build your design without guessing.

lessons.title: Components, variants and properties: building a reusable library
objectives: Create main components and use instances with overrides correctly
Combine variants into a component set with clear property names
Use boolean, text and instance swap properties to keep variant counts low
Choose a Figma plan, plugins and Community kits suited to your stage

blocks.text: A **component** is an element you build once and reuse: a button, an input field, a product card, a bottom navigation bar. The original is the **main component** (purple diamond icon in the layers panel). Every copy is an **instance**. Change the main component and every instance updates across the file. In an instance you can still **override** some things, such as the label text or an icon, without breaking the link. This is what lets one designer keep 40 screens consistent.

blocks.name: design-components
blocks.alt: Interface components arranged as reusable building blocks
blocks.caption: A component library is a set of building blocks: build each piece once, reuse it on every screen.

blocks.text: Tools and setup for this stage

items: **Plan**: the free Starter plan is enough to learn and build a portfolio. Paid plans add things such as unlimited shared files, team libraries and Dev Mode. Students and teachers can apply for the free Education plan. Check figma.com/pricing for current limits before you promise a client anything that depends on a paid feature.
**Desktop app**: lighter on browser memory and lets you use fonts installed on your computer. The browser works too.

**Community kits**: Google's Material 3 Design Kit and Apple's iOS UI kits are published on the Figma Community. Study how they name and structure components; do not ship them unchanged as your own work.

**Plugins** (Main menu, Plugins): a contrast checker, an icon plugin such as Iconify, and a stock photo plugin such as Unsplash cover most needs. Install only plugins from known publishers and never paste client passwords or private data into a plugin.

blocks.text: From element to component set

items: Build the element with auto layout and your saved styles only (no loose colours).
Select it and press Ctrl + Alt + K (Mac: Cmd + Option + K). Name it with a slash path, for example "Button".
Duplicate the main component for each version you need, select all of them and click **Combine as variants**. Figma wraps them in a dashed purple **component set**.
In the right panel, rename the default property "Property 1" to something meaningful, such as **Type**, and give each value a clear name: Primary, Secondary, Ghost.
Add more variant properties only when the look truly changes, for example **State** (Default, Pressed, Disabled) and **Size** (Medium, Large).
Use the other property types to avoid duplicating variants: **Text** (edit the label from the panel), **Boolean** (show or hide an icon), **Instance swap** (choose which icon).

blocks.title: Worked example: keeping the button set small
blocks.context: For example, Amaka needs Oja Fresh buttons in 3 types, 3 states and 2 sizes, and some buttons need a leading icon (a cart or a plus sign).
steps: Variants needed without icons: 3 types × 3 states × 2 sizes = 18 variants.
If she made "with icon" a variant too, the count doubles: 18 × 2 = 36 variants, and every future change must be made 36 times over.
Instead she puts an icon instance in every variant and adds a **Boolean** property "Show icon" linked to the icon layer's visibility. The count stays at 18.
She adds an **Instance swap** property "Icon" so a designer can choose cart, plus or arrow from the panel without detaching.
She adds a **Text** property "Label" linked to the text layer, so the label is edited from the right panel.
She tests: places an instance on the Home screen, switches Type to Secondary, turns Show icon on, swaps the icon to plus and types "Add to cart". The button hugs the longer label.
blocks.result: One component set with 18 variants and three extra properties covers every button in the app, instead of 36 hand-maintained copies.

blocks.title: How a design system is layered
items: Screens
Patterns: checkout, product list
Components: button, input, card
Styles and variables
Foundation values: colour, type, space
blocks.caption: Each layer is built only from the layer beneath it, so a change at the base flows up to every screen.

blocks.text: Naming and organising the library

Put all main components on the **Components** page, grouped in sections: Actions (buttons, icon buttons), Inputs (text field, dropdown, checkbox), Display (product card, badge, price tag), Navigation (top bar, bottom nav, tabs). Slash names such as "Input/Text field" create folders in the Assets panel. Add a short description to each main component, such as "Use Primary for one main action per screen", because that text appears to anyone who inserts it.

blocks.title: Detaching is a last resort
blocks.text: Detach instance (Ctrl + Alt + B, Mac Cmd + Option + B) breaks the link to the main component. The detached copy will never receive future fixes. If you keep wanting to detach, your component is missing a property or a variant; fix the component instead.
Variables for modes and tokens

Figma **variables** store reusable values of four types: colour, number, string and boolean. A collection can have **modes**, for example Light and Dark, so the same variable "Color/Surface" is white in Light and near-black in Dark. Number variables are ideal for spacing and radius tokens (Space/16, Radius/12). Developers can read these names in their code later, which is a big step towards a shared language between design and code. Check your plan's limits on how many modes you can create.

takeaways: Main component changes flow to every instance; overrides customise without breaking the link.
Use variants only for real visual changes; use boolean, text and instance swap properties for the rest.
3 × 3 × 2 = 18 variants is manageable; doubling for small options is not.
Organise components in sections with slash names and descriptions.

activity.title: Build your first component set
steps: Build a button with auto layout using only your saved styles.
Make variants for at least 2 types and 3 states and combine them into a component set with named properties.
Add a Boolean property for an icon, an Instance swap property for which icon, and a Text property for the label.
Build one more component (text input or product card) with Default, Focused and Error variants.
Replace hand-made elements on your screen with instances and test every property.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your Components page and of the right panel showing the properties of one selected instance.

lessons.title: Interactive prototypes: flows, triggers, overlays and Smart Animate
objectives: Set a flow starting point and connect screens with triggers and actions
Use overlays, scroll behaviour and fixed elements for realistic mobile behaviour
Apply Smart Animate and interactive components with matching layer names
Test a prototype on a real phone and share it safely with a client

blocks.text: A **prototype** links your static screens so people can tap through them as if the app were real. It is how a client approves the experience before paying for development, and how you catch problems such as a missing "back" path. In Figma you build it in the **Prototype** tab of the right panel, using the same frames you designed.

blocks.name: mobile-prototyping
blocks.alt: A person linking mobile screens into a clickable prototype
blocks.caption: A prototype turns separate screens into one experience a client can hold and tap.

blocks.text: The vocabulary of a connection

head: Part
Meaning
Common choices
rows: On tap (On click), While pressing, On drag, After delay
Navigate to, Back, Open overlay, Close overlay, Swap overlay, Scroll to, Change to, Open link
Another frame, an overlay frame, or a section of the same frame
Instant, Dissolve, Smart animate, Move in, Push, Slide in
Ease out, around 200 to 300 ms for most mobile transitions

blocks.text: Select a layer, drag the blue circle on its edge to a destination frame, and a connection appears with these settings. A **flow** starts from a frame you mark as the starting point; you can have several flows in one file, for example "Buy tomatoes" and "Track an order", each with its own name and shareable link.

blocks.title: The Buy tomatoes prototype flow
items: Home
Product detail
Quantity bottom sheet
Cart
Checkout
Order confirmed
blocks.caption: Six frames, one starting point, with an overlay for choosing quantity instead of a separate screen.

blocks.title: Worked example: wiring the Oja Fresh checkout
blocks.context: For example, Amaka prototypes the main purchase journey on the Prototype page, using duplicates of her final screens so the design pages stay clean.
steps: Marks "Home / Default" as the flow starting point and names the flow "Buy tomatoes".
Product card on Home: On tap, Navigate to "Product / Tomatoes", animation Move in from right, Ease out, 250 ms.
"Add to cart" button: On tap, Open overlay "Sheet / Quantity", position Bottom center, with "Close when clicking outside" ticked and a dark background at 40 percent opacity.
Inside the sheet, "Confirm" button: On tap, Navigate to "Cart / One item". The sheet closes automatically because the base screen changes.
Back arrow on every inner screen: On tap, Back. She uses Back instead of linking to a named screen, so the path always matches how the user arrived.
"Pay ₦6,500" on Checkout (sample amount): On tap, Navigate to "Checkout / Processing", then that frame uses After delay 1500 ms, Navigate to "Order / Confirmed", Dissolve.
Counts her connections: 8 in total, and checks each one in presentation mode.
blocks.result: A client can now complete a full purchase on her phone in under a minute, including a realistic quantity sheet and processing pause.

blocks.text: Scrolling and fixed elements

Phone screens scroll. Make the Home frame taller than the device if the content needs it, or keep the device height and let the content overflow with clipping on. Then set **vertical scrolling** for the frame (overflow behaviour). Select the top app bar and bottom navigation and set their position to **Fixed** (or **Sticky** for a header that scrolls up and then sticks) so they stay in place while the list moves. A prototype where the bottom navigation scrolls away looks broken to clients.
Smart Animate and interactive components

**Smart animate** looks for layers with the **same name** in the start and end frames and animates the differences in position, size, colour and opacity. If the cart badge is called "Badge" in both frames and its number changes from 1 to 2, it will animate smoothly. If one is called "Badge" and the other "Ellipse 3", it will just jump. Keep names identical.

**Interactive components** add behaviour inside a component set. In your Button set, connect the Default variant to the Pressed variant with While pressing, Change to. Every instance in every screen now shows the pressed state automatically. The same works for checkboxes (On tap, Change to Checked) and favourite icons.
Presenting the prototype to a client

Do not just send a link and wait. Book a 30-minute call, share your screen and walk through each flow as the user would, saying out loud what the person is trying to do: "Bisi wants two paint buckets of tomatoes delivered before 6 pm." Then hand control to the client on their own phone and watch where they hesitate. Write down every comment, group them by screen afterwards, and send back one list of agreed changes. Click the Present button (the play icon) and use the device frame option so the prototype looks like a real phone on screen.

blocks.title: Test on a real phone
blocks.text: Install the Figma mobile app, sign in, and open the prototype from your files or the share link. Small-screen problems, tiny tap targets and slow-feeling transitions show up immediately on a real device that you would miss on a laptop.

blocks.title: Share prototypes safely
blocks.text: Use Share prototype and set access to "can view" only. Use sample names, addresses and phone numbers in your screens, never real customer data from the client's records. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 applies to personal data, and a public link can be forwarded beyond the people you meant to show.

takeaways: Every connection is trigger, action, destination and animation.
Use overlays for sheets and dialogs, Back for back arrows, and named flows for each journey.
Set scrolling on long screens and Fixed position on bars that must stay put.
Smart animate only works when matching layers share exactly the same name.

activity.title: Prototype one complete journey
steps: Pick one journey in your practice app with at least five screens and mark a named flow starting point.
Connect every screen, including Back actions, with consistent animation and duration.
Add at least one overlay (bottom sheet or dialog) and one fixed bar on a scrolling screen.
Make your button component interactive with a pressed state.
Test the whole flow on your phone in the Figma mobile app and fix any dead end.
activity.evidence: A short screen recording (30 to 60 seconds) of the prototype running on your phone, or a screenshot of the Prototype tab connections plus the view-only link.

lessons.title: Quality checks and developer handoff: contrast, targets, naming and specs
objectives: Calculate and check text and non-text contrast against WCAG 2.2 AA thresholds
Audit tap target sizes, text resizing and states before handover
Prepare layers, exports and annotations so a developer can build without guessing
Run a handoff using Dev Mode on paid plans, or a clear spec page on the free plan

blocks.text: A design can look beautiful and still be unusable or unbuildable. Before any handover, run a **quality pass**: accessibility checks, consistency checks and file hygiene. Then prepare the file so the developer reads values from it instead of guessing from a screenshot. This lesson gives you a repeatable checklist.

blocks.name: code-inspection
blocks.alt: A person inspecting interface code and specifications
blocks.caption: Handoff succeeds when a developer can inspect the file and find every value they need.

blocks.text: Colour contrast: the numbers

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.2) set minimum **contrast ratios** for level AA, the level most organisations aim for: **4.5 : 1** for normal text, **3 : 1** for large text (about 24 px regular or 18.7 px bold and above), and **3 : 1** for important non-text parts such as input borders and icons that carry meaning. The ratio is (L1 + 0.05) ÷ (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the relative luminance of the lighter colour and L2 of the darker. White has luminance 1.

blocks.title: Worked example: auditing four Oja Fresh colour pairs
blocks.context: For example, before handover Amaka checks the pairs used most on her screens with a contrast checker plugin, and confirms one by hand.
steps: By hand: grey #757575 has relative luminance of about 0.178. On white: (1 + 0.05) ÷ (0.178 + 0.05) = 1.05 ÷ 0.228 = about 4.6 : 1. Passes 4.5 for normal text, just.
Same grey on her light card background #F5F5F5: the plugin shows about 4.2 : 1. Fails for normal text. She switches secondary text to #616161, about 6.2 : 1 on white.
White text on the green primary button #2E7D32: about 5.1 : 1. Passes.
White text on an orange promo tag #EF6C00: about 3.1 : 1. Fails for 13 px text. She darkens it to #BF360C, about 5.6 : 1.
Input border #BDBDBD on white: about 1.9 : 1. Fails the 3 : 1 non-text rule, so users may not see where to type. She darkens the border to #757575.
blocks.result: Three of five pairs needed fixing. Each fix took one edit to a colour variable, and every screen updated at once.

blocks.title: Same colour, different result
blocks.text: Contrast depends on both colours. A grey that passes on white can fail on light grey. Always check text against the actual background it sits on.
The pre-handover checklist

blocks.title: Pre-handover quality pass
items: Text contrast 4.5:1 checked
Tap targets 48 or larger
All states designed
Layers named, no strays
Exports set on assets
Prototype has no dead ends
blocks.caption: Run this list on every screen before you mark anything ready for development.

items: **Tap targets**: interactive areas at least 48 × 48 on Android (44 × 44 points on iOS). An icon can be 24 px if its tappable frame is 48. WCAG 2.2 also sets a minimum target size of 24 × 24 CSS pixels at AA.
**Text resizing**: increase body text by 30 percent on a test copy of one screen. Do buttons and cards grow without overlapping? Auto layout with Hug makes this pass.
**States**: every input has Default, Focused, Filled, Error and Disabled; every list has an empty state; every data screen has loading and error states.
**Not colour alone**: an error is shown by colour plus an icon and a message, so colour-blind users still see it.
**Consistency**: Figma's Selection colors section shows every colour used in a selection; anything not linked to a style or variable is a stray to fix.

blocks.text: Preparing assets and specs

Select each icon or illustration the developer needs, add an **export setting** and choose the format: **SVG** for icons and simple vector art, **PNG** or **WebP** handled by the developer for photos. For raster assets on Android, developers often need several densities (1x mdpi, 1.5x hdpi, 2x xhdpi, 3x xxhdpi, 4x xxxhdpi); on iOS, 1x, 2x and 3x. Agree this with the developer first; many teams now use SVG icons and let code handle sizes. Name export layers clearly, for example "ic_cart", because the layer name becomes the file name.

head: Handoff route
When
What you do
rows: Client or team has a paid seat for the developer
Mark sections "Ready for dev", add annotations with measurements and notes, link components to code where set up
Free plan or a developer without a Figma seat
Add a Handoff page with redlines (spacing and sizes drawn on a copy of each key screen), a table of colour and type values, and exported assets in a shared folder

blocks.title: Write the notes you would want
blocks.text: Annotate behaviour that a static screen cannot show: "Phone number field accepts 11 digits starting with 0", "Disable Pay button until delivery address is chosen", "Show cached prices if offline". These sentences prevent most back-and-forth messages.

Finish with a 20-minute **handoff walk-through** call with the developer: share the file, open each flow, point to the components page and the notes, and save a named version "Handoff v1". After that, put any change in a new named version and tell the developer exactly what moved.

takeaways: AA contrast: 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text and key non-text elements.
Check text against its real background; the same grey can pass on white and fail on light grey.
Design every state and keep targets at least 48 × 48 (44 points on iOS).
Hand off with Dev Mode on paid plans, or a clear spec page and exported assets on the free plan.

activity.title: Run a pre-handover audit
steps: List the five colour pairs used most in your practice app and check each with a contrast plugin; fix any that fail.
Check every tappable element on two screens for a 48 × 48 target and fix small ones.
Rename all layers on one screen and remove hidden or empty layers.
Add export settings to all icons on that screen and export them as SVG.
Write at least five behaviour annotations for the developer and save a version named "Handoff v1".
activity.evidence: A table of your colour pairs with before and after ratios, plus a screenshot of the annotated screen.

quiz.q: Amaka needs buttons in 3 types, 3 states and 2 sizes, with an optional icon. What is the best way to handle the icon?
options: Add a Boolean property linked to the icon layer, keeping 18 variants
Add a variant property Icon=Yes/No, giving 36 variants
Detach instances that need an icon and add it by hand
Make a separate component set for icon buttons with 18 more variants
quiz.explain: A boolean property shows or hides the icon without doubling the variant count from 18 to 36.

quiz.q: A designer keeps detaching button instances to change the label colour for one screen. What is the real fix?
options: Add the needed look as a variant or property of the main component
Copy and paste the button from another file
Turn the button into a group
quiz.explain: Frequent detaching means the component is missing a variant or property. Fix the component so instances keep receiving updates.

quiz.q: In the prototype, the cart badge number jumps instead of animating, even though Smart animate is set. What is the most likely cause?
options: Smart animate only works on desktop
The badge layer has different names in the two frames
quiz.explain: Smart animate matches layers by name. Different names mean it cannot pair them, so it switches instantly.

quiz.q: Secondary text #757575 measures about 4.6:1 on white but about 4.2:1 on the card background #F5F5F5. The text is 13 px. What should the designer do?
options: Use a darker grey such as #616161 or change the background
Make the text bold at 13 px
quiz.explain: Normal text needs 4.5:1 against its actual background. On #F5F5F5 it fails, so darken the text or change the background.

quiz.q: The client's developer has no paid Figma seat. What is the most professional handoff?
options: Tell the developer to estimate spacing by eye
A spec page with redlines, a value table, behaviour notes and exported assets
Wait until the client buys every seat
quiz.explain: A clear spec page plus exported assets gives exact values on any plan.

quiz.q: Which connection is best for the back arrow on an inner screen?
quiz.explain: Back returns users to wherever they came from, so the path always matches how they arrived.

modules.title: Clients, Pricing and Your UI Portfolio
modules.overview: You learn to run discovery for a UI project, turn it into a screen inventory and a priced proposal with clear limits, and present your work as a portfolio case study backed by a well-organised Figma file and a 90-day plan for paid work.

lessons.title: Client discovery for UI projects: brand, platform, content and build questions
objectives: Run a structured discovery call covering brand, users, platform, content and development
Classify a project by how ready its brand and UX are
Turn discovery notes into a screen inventory with states
Spot red flags that signal hidden scope before you quote

blocks.text: Most UI projects that go wrong were unclear from the first conversation. A client says "I need an app design" and means something very different from what you imagine. **Discovery** is a short, structured conversation, usually 45 to 60 minutes, that turns a vague request into a defined list of screens, components and deliverables you can price. You are not designing yet; you are finding out what must be designed and what already exists.

blocks.name: questions
blocks.alt: A person with question marks thinking through a problem
blocks.caption: Good discovery questions uncover the real scope before you quote a price.

blocks.text: Five areas to cover

head: Area
Questions to ask
What you are listening for
rows: Do you have a logo, colours, fonts or brand guidelines? Can you send the files?
Whether you are building on an existing identity or also creating one
Who uses this and what are the three most important things they do? Has anyone mapped the flows or made wireframes?
Whether UX work is done, partly done or missing
Android, iPhone, web, or all three? Which phones do your customers use most?
Screen sizes, platform conventions (Material or iOS), number of layouts per screen
Who writes the text? Do you have real product photos and prices?
Whether you will wait for content, or design with sample content that must be replaced
Who is building it, and with what (Flutter, React Native, native Android, a website builder)? Does the developer use Figma?
Handoff route, export formats, whether Dev Mode or a spec page is needed

blocks.text: Also ask who gives final approval and how feedback will arrive. "My partner and my sister will both review" means two sets of opinions per round. Ask for one decision-maker and one consolidated list of comments per round, and write that into your proposal.

blocks.title: How ready is this project for UI work?
items: UX ready, no brand: add light brand work
UX ready, brand ready: pure UI build
Neither ready: start with discovery and UX
Brand ready, no UX: map flows first
blocks.caption: Where a client sits on these two axes changes what you must deliver and therefore what you charge.

blocks.title: Worked example: from a discovery call to a screen inventory
blocks.context: For example, Kemi runs a tailoring studio in Ibadan and wants an Android app where customers book fittings, save their measurements and track orders. Her developer will build in Flutter. She has a logo and two brand colours, but no fonts or guidelines, and no wireframes.
steps: Classifies the project: brand partly ready, UX missing. So the quote must include simple user flows before screens, and a small brand foundation (fonts, extra colours, type scale).
Lists the three main tasks Kemi named: book a fitting, save measurements, track an order.

Writes the screen inventory: Welcome, Sign up with phone number, Home, Book fitting (date and time), Booking confirmed, Measurements form, Measurements saved view, Orders list, Order detail with status steps, Profile and settings. That is 10 screens.
Adds required states: empty Orders list, Measurements form error, no-network message on Home, booking slot unavailable. That is 4 extra state frames.
Notes components needed: button set, text input set, date chip, time slot chip, order status stepper, order card, bottom navigation.
Notes platform: Android only, Material conventions, test at 360 and 412 px wide. Handoff: developer has no paid seat, so a spec page is needed.
Sends Kemi a one-page summary the same day and asks her to confirm it before any quote.
blocks.result: A vague "app design" request became 10 screens, 4 states, 7 components and a known handoff route, all confirmed in writing before pricing.

blocks.text: Red flags that hide extra work

items: "Just make it like Jumia or Opay": copying a large company's app means dozens of screens and features. Ask which three screens matter most.
"We will send the content later": plan sample content and say in writing that replacing it is a separate task.
"Design it for phone, tablet and web": each layout multiplies screen count. Price each platform separately.
"Can you also do the logo?": brand identity is a separate project with its own price.
No named decision-maker: expect endless rounds of feedback unless you set limits.

blocks.text: When the product already exists

Many UI jobs are redesigns, not new apps. Then discovery also means an **inventory of what is already there**. Ask for screenshots of every current screen (or install the app and capture them yourself), any existing Figma or design files, and the developer's existing component code if there is any. Lay the screenshots side by side on a Figma page and count how many different button styles, font sizes and greys are in use. Finding, for example, seven button styles where two would do is concrete evidence for a foundations and components line in your quote. Also ask what customers complain about most, because those screens should be redesigned first.

blocks.title: Record decisions, not just conversations
blocks.text: After every call, send a short written summary on email or WhatsApp: what was agreed, what is open, and the next step. If the client later says "I thought you were doing the tablet version", you can point to the summary they confirmed.

takeaways: Discovery turns a vague request into screens, states, components and a handoff route.
Always ask about brand, users and flows, platform, content and the developer's tools.
Classify brand and UX readiness; missing pieces are extra work to price.
Confirm the screen inventory in writing before you quote.

activity.title: Run a practice discovery
steps: Ask a friend or small business owner to role-play a client who wants an app or website.
Run a 30-minute call using the five areas in the table, and take notes.
Place the project in the readiness matrix and write one sentence explaining why.
Write a screen inventory with states and a component list.
Send a one-page written summary and ask them to confirm or correct it.
activity.evidence: Your discovery notes and the one-page summary with the screen inventory.

lessons.title: Pricing UI work: screen-based estimates, design-system fees and change control
objectives: Estimate hours from a screen inventory using complexity weights
Price design-system work, prototyping and handoff as separate line items
Write proposal terms for revision rounds, change requests and staged payments
Protect yourself from common payment scams and file misuse

blocks.text: Most UI projects suit **fixed project pricing**: a defined set of screens, components and deliverables for a set price. The danger is that "a set of screens" grows. The answer is a transparent estimate built from your screen inventory, with clear limits and a price for anything extra. Clients accept limits far more easily when they can see how the number was built.

blocks.name: pricing-page
blocks.alt: A pricing page showing different packages
blocks.caption: A clear, itemised price helps a client see what they are paying for and what costs extra.

blocks.text: Fixed, hourly or retainer?

head: Model
Best when
Risk to manage
rows: Scope is clear and the screen inventory is confirmed
Scope creep; control it with written rounds and change requests
Scope is unclear, or you are joining an existing team to help
Client worries about open-ended cost; send weekly time reports
Ongoing design for a live product: new features, fixes, marketing screens
Unused or overused hours; agree a monthly hour cap and what happens to extra requests

blocks.text: To set your own hourly figure, start from what you need to earn each month, add business costs (data, electricity or fuel for a generator, laptop replacement, software), and divide by the hours you can realistically bill. Most freelancers bill far fewer hours than they work, because discovery calls, proposals and admin are unpaid time. Then compare the result with what local clients in your target market can pay, and adjust your offer rather than working below your costs.
Step 1: weight each screen
Not all screens take the same effort. Track your own time on practice projects so your weights are honest. A simple starting scale, which you should adjust to your real speed:

head: Complexity
Examples
Starting estimate per screen
rows: Home, list, profile, booking confirmation with details
Multi-field forms, checkout, dashboards, status trackers

blocks.text: Step 2: add the work that is not screens

items: **Foundations and component library**: often the biggest single block on a new product, because every screen depends on it. Price it separately so the client sees its value.
**Prototype**: wiring, testing on a phone and fixing dead ends.
**Handoff**: annotations, spec page or Dev Mode preparation, exports and the walk-through call.
**Buffer**: 10 to 20 percent for the unknowns every project has.

blocks.title: Worked example: quoting Kemi's tailoring app
blocks.context: For example, using the inventory from the last lesson (10 screens plus 4 state frames), and an illustrative rate of ₦10,000 per hour. This rate is an example only, not a market figure; set your own from your costs, skill and local demand.
steps: Screens: 3 simple × 3 h = 9 h; 5 medium × 5 h = 25 h; 2 complex (Measurements form, Order detail tracker) × 8 h = 16 h. Screens total 50 h.
State frames: 4 × 2 h = 8 h (they reuse the parent screen).
Foundations and component library (7 components with states): 16 h. Simple user flows before design, because UX was missing: 6 h.
Prototype: 6 h. Handoff spec page and walk-through: 5 h.
Subtotal: 50 + 8 + 16 + 6 + 6 + 5 = 91 h. Buffer 15 percent: 91 × 0.15 = 13.65 h, so total about 105 h.
Staged payments: 50 percent deposit ₦525,000; 30 percent on approval of key screens ₦315,000; 20 percent at handoff ₦210,000. Check: 525,000 + 315,000 + 210,000 = ₦1,050,000.
blocks.result: A quote the client can read line by line. If Kemi wants to save money she can remove a line (for example the prototype), instead of pushing the total down with nothing removed.

blocks.title: Payments tied to milestones
items: Signed proposal, 50% deposit
Foundations and components
Key screens approved, 30%
Remaining screens and prototype
Handoff and final 20%
blocks.caption: Each payment unlocks the next stage, so neither side carries all the risk.

blocks.text: Terms that control scope

items: **Included**: list every screen by name, the platforms, the components and the deliverables (Figma file, prototype link, spec page, exported assets).
**Revision rounds**: for example, two rounds of consolidated feedback per stage. A round is one written list from the named decision-maker.
**Change requests**: new screens or features are quoted with the same weights. A new medium screen in this example is 5 h × ₦10,000 = ₦50,000.
**Content**: client supplies final text and photos by an agreed date; design uses sample content until then.
**Ownership**: edit access to the final file (or transfer of the file to the client's team) on final payment. Until then the client views by link.
**Timeline**: dates depend on feedback arriving within an agreed number of working days.

blocks.title: Money scams aimed at freelancers
blocks.text: Be wary of a new "client" who sends more money than agreed and asks you to refund the difference, or who sends a payment screenshot or SMS alert instead of money you can see in your bank or wallet app. Confirm every payment inside your bank, Paystack, Moniepoint or Opay account before you start or deliver. Never share your BVN, OTPs or banking PIN with a client. For international clients, use invoices on recognised platforms and read their fee and withdrawal terms first.

blocks.title: Keep the file in your workspace until final payment
blocks.text: Work in your own Figma team, share view-only links during the project, and move or duplicate the file to the client's workspace after the final payment, as your proposal states.

takeaways: Build quotes from the screen inventory with honest complexity weights.
Price foundations and components, prototype and handoff as separate lines, plus a buffer.
Define rounds, change requests and ownership in writing.
Tie payments to milestones and confirm every payment in your own account.

activity.title: Write a priced proposal
steps: Use your screen inventory from the last activity and give each screen a complexity weight.
Add lines for foundations and components, prototype, handoff and a 10 to 20 percent buffer.
Choose an hourly figure based on your own costs and goals, and calculate the total, showing your arithmetic.
Split the total into three staged payments and check they add up.
Write the scope terms: included items, revision rounds, change request price, content, ownership and timeline.
activity.evidence: A one or two page proposal document with the itemised estimate and terms.

lessons.title: Your UI portfolio: a case study, an inspectable Figma file and a 90-day plan
objectives: Choose two or three projects that show systems thinking, not just pretty screens
Write a UI case study that explains decisions with evidence
Prepare a view-only Figma file that reviewers can inspect with confidence
Set a 90-day plan aimed at in-house, agency or freelance work

blocks.text: Hiring managers and clients who know UI work look past the final screens. They want to see **how** you work: is there a real component system, are layers named, are states designed, did you check contrast, can you explain why you chose a layout? Your portfolio should answer those questions before they ask.

blocks.name: portfolio-website
blocks.alt: A designer's portfolio website on screen
blocks.caption: A strong UI portfolio shows finished screens and the system and reasoning behind them.

blocks.text: Where UI designers find work

head: Path
What they look for
Portfolio emphasis
rows: In-house product teams (fintech, e-commerce, health, education, logistics)
Working inside an existing design system with developers and product managers
Speed across different clients and brands
Range of visual styles, clean files, deadlines met
A usable app or website that looks professional and is delivered on time
Before and after, clear pricing, testimonials from real clients
Remote international work (LinkedIn, Upwork, Contra and similar)
Clear written English, time-zone reliability, polished case studies
Strong written case studies and responsive communication

blocks.text: What to include

items: **Two or three complete projects**: real client work if you have it, or well-scoped practice projects such as Oja Fresh. Depth beats quantity.
**At least one full case study** with problem, constraints, process, decisions and result.
**A view-only Figma link** for at least one project, so reviewers can inspect your components, naming and prototype.
**A prototype link or short screen recording** of a real flow on a phone.
Only honest claims. If a project is a concept, say so. Never present someone else's Community file as your own.

blocks.title: Worked example: outlining the Oja Fresh case study
blocks.context: For example, Amaka writes her case study as a one-page web post with images, following six headings. She labels it clearly as a practice concept.
steps: **Overview**: "A concept app for ordering foodstuff from local markets for home delivery. Solo project, 4 weeks, Figma."
**Problem and constraints**: users on 360 px Android phones, outdoors in daylight, careful with data; prices change often.

**Foundations**: shows her 8-point spacing set, the type scale arithmetic (16 × 1.25 steps, rounded) and colour roles, with the contrast fixes she made (secondary grey from #757575 to #616161 on light cards).
**Components**: a screenshot of the Button set (18 variants, plus Show icon, Icon and Label properties) and the product card, with one sentence on why she used a boolean instead of 18 more variants.
**Key decisions**: the quantity bottom sheet instead of a separate screen, explained in two sentences, with before and after images.
**Result and next steps**: prototype link, file link, and what she would test with real users next. No invented metrics.
blocks.result: A reviewer understands in two minutes what she built, why, and how carefully, and can open the file to check.

blocks.title: Your 90-day plan
items: Days 1-30: finish two projects
Days 31-45: write case studies
Days 46-60: publish portfolio
Days 61-90: 30 targeted applications
blocks.caption: Build the evidence first, then present it, then go after specific opportunities every week.

blocks.text: What experienced reviewers check in your file

items: Do screens use component instances, or are buttons drawn by hand on every screen?
Are colours and text linked to styles or variables, or are there loose hex values everywhere?
Are layers and frames named, and are auto layout frames used for lists, cards and buttons?
Are empty, loading and error states designed, not just the happy path?
Does the prototype run from start to finish without dead ends?
Can they follow the file without you explaining it?

blocks.text: Prepare the file people will inspect

items: Duplicate the project file and remove client-confidential content or anything you do not have permission to show.
Check the cover, page names, sections and component descriptions.
Set the share link to "Anyone with the link can view" and test it in a private browser window while logged out.
Point the case study to specific pages: "Components page shows the full button set."

blocks.text: Then pick **one target**: in-house product roles, agencies, or freelance for a specific client type such as restaurants, schools or fashion brands. A focused portfolio and message beat a general one. For freelance targets, offer a small fixed-price starter service, such as redesigning three key screens with a component set, so a new client can try you with low risk.

When you reach out, keep messages short and specific. Name the company or business, mention one screen of theirs you noticed and one concrete improvement you could make, link the most relevant case study, and propose a 15-minute call. Ten personal messages a week, each linked to a relevant piece of your work, usually get further than a hundred copy-paste ones. Track every message, reply and follow-up in a simple spreadsheet so you can see what is working by day 90.

blocks.title: Ask permission for client work
blocks.text: Before publishing any client project, ask in writing whether you may show it, and whether names or data must be hidden. Some clients allow it only after launch.

takeaways: Show the system behind the screens: foundations, components, states and handoff.
One honest, well-structured case study beats many unexplained images.
Share a tidy view-only Figma file and test the link while logged out.
Choose one target path and act on it every week for 90 days.

activity.title: Publish your first case study
steps: Choose your strongest project and write the six case study headings with notes under each.
Capture images: foundations, component set, two key screens and one before and after decision.
Prepare a view-only copy of the Figma file and test the link while logged out.
Publish the case study on a portfolio site, Behance, LinkedIn or a free website builder.
Write your 90-day plan with one target path and weekly actions.
activity.evidence: The link to your published case study, the view-only Figma link and your written 90-day plan.

quiz.q: A client has a logo and colours but no user flows or wireframes. What should your UI proposal include?
options: Only final screens, since the brand is ready
Simple user flows before screen design, priced as a line item
Nothing until the client hires a UX researcher
quiz.explain: Brand is partly ready but UX is missing, so the flows must be done first and priced as part of the job.

quiz.q: Using the course weights, how many hours are 2 simple, 4 medium and 1 complex screens?
A total project price is ₦800,000. With a 50/30/20 payment plan, how much is the final payment at handoff?
A new client sends a screenshot of a bank alert for more than the deposit and asks you to refund the extra. What should you do?
options: Refund the extra quickly to build trust
Confirm the payment inside your own bank or payment app before doing anything
Ask them to send another screenshot
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked. Only money you can see in your own account is real.

quiz.q: Which portfolio item best shows a reviewer your systems thinking?
options: A view-only Figma link with named components, states and a case study explaining decisions
A list of tools you know
A Community UI kit you downloaded
quiz.explain: Reviewers want to inspect real components, naming and decisions, which the file and case study show.

quiz.q: The client asks for a tablet layout after signing a phone-only proposal. What is the professional response?
options: Do it for free to keep them happy
Quote it as a change request using the same weights
Stretch the phone screens to tablet width without telling them
quiz.explain: Extra platforms multiply screens. Your proposal's change request terms let you price it fairly.

finalQuiz.q: Which container should you use for a horizontal row of chips that must re-space automatically when a chip is added?
finalQuiz.explain: Auto layout stacks children by gap and padding, so new items slot in without manual re-spacing.

finalQuiz.q: A search bar inside a normal frame should stretch when the screen gets wider. Which horizontal constraint fits?
finalQuiz.explain: Left and right pins both edges, so the bar stretches with the frame.

finalQuiz.q: A screen is 360 px wide with 16 px margins on each side. How wide is the content area?
With base 16 and ratio 1.2, what is the next size up?
finalQuiz.explain: 16 × 1.2 = 19.2, which you might round to 19 or 20.

finalQuiz.q: Why name a colour style "Text/Secondary" instead of "Grey 600"?
options: Role names keep meaning when the value changes in a rebrand
finalQuiz.explain: Naming by role lets values change while every element keeps the right purpose.

finalQuiz.q: A card component needs an optional "Sale" badge. What keeps the variant count lowest?
options: A Boolean property controlling the badge's visibility
A new variant for every card with a badge
Detaching cards that need a badge
A separate file for sale cards
finalQuiz.explain: A boolean property shows or hides the badge without duplicating variants.

finalQuiz.q: Which action best suits a quantity picker that slides up over the product screen?
finalQuiz.explain: Open overlay shows a sheet on top of the current screen, which matches a bottom sheet.

finalQuiz.q: The bottom navigation scrolls away with the list in the prototype. What fixes it?
finalQuiz.explain: Fixed position keeps the bar in place while the frame content scrolls.

finalQuiz.q: White text on an orange tag measures about 3.1:1 and the text is 13 px. Under WCAG 2.2 AA, what is the verdict?
options: Passes if the tag is rounded
finalQuiz.explain: 13 px is normal-size text, which needs at least 4.5:1. 3:1 applies only to large text and key non-text elements.

finalQuiz.q: What minimum touch target is recommended on Android?
finalQuiz.explain: Material Design recommends at least 48 × 48 for touch targets; Apple recommends 44 × 44 points.

finalQuiz.q: An inventory has 4 simple, 3 medium and 2 complex screens. Using 3, 5 and 8 hours, what is the screen total before other work and buffer?
Before sharing a portfolio Figma link, what should you do?
options: Make it editable so reviewers can try things
Remove confidential content, set view-only access and test the link while logged out
finalQuiz.explain: A tidy, view-only, tested link lets reviewers inspect your work without exposing client data or your file.

capstone.title: UI Design Portfolio Project
capstone.brief: Design a complete multi-screen mobile interface for a practice or real client app in Figma, built on your own foundations and component system, linked as a working prototype, handed off with specs, and presented as a case study with a pricing proposal for similar client work.
steps: Write a short brief and screen inventory (at least 8 screens plus their key states) for an app idea relevant to your community.
Set up the file with Cover, Foundations, Components, Screens, Prototype and Handoff pages.
Define spacing, a calculated type scale and colour roles as styles or variables.
Build at least five components with variants and properties (button, input, card, navigation and one more).
Design all screens from instances, test at 360 px and 412 px, and design empty, error and loading states.
Wire one complete journey as a prototype with an overlay and fixed bars, and test it on your phone.
Run the contrast and target-size audit, fix failures, add annotations and export assets.
Write a case study and an itemised pricing proposal for building a similar app for a client.
evidence: View-only Figma link with named pages, sections, layers and components
Prototype link or a 60-second screen recording on a phone
Contrast audit table with before and after ratios
Handoff page or Dev Mode annotations with exported assets
Pricing proposal with screen weights, line items, staged payments and scope terms
